```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
post_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = post_dir)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis
#| include: false
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

for (folder in c("data/raw", "data/clean", "figures", "results")) {
  dir.create(folder, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
}

page_numbers <- 1:24

scrape_hockey_page <- function(page_number) {
  url <- paste0("https://www.scrapethissite.com/pages/forms/?page_num=",
                page_number)
  file <- file.path("data/raw", sprintf("page_%02d.html", page_number))
  record_file <- paste0(file, ".csv")

  if (!file.exists(file)) {
    Sys.sleep(1)
    page <- read_html(url)
    # Stop on unexpected content rather than trying to evade access controls.
    if (length(html_elements(page, "tr.team")) == 0) {
      stop("No team rows on page ", page_number,
           ". Check the site manually; do not bypass access restrictions.")
    }
    xml2::write_html(page, file)
    write_csv(tibble(page_number = page_number, source_url = url,
                     retrieved_at = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z")),
              record_file)
  } else {
    page <- read_html(file)
  }

  if (!file.exists(record_file)) {
    stop("Missing retrieval record for ", file)
  }
  rows <- html_elements(page, "tr.team")
  if (length(rows) == 0) stop("No team rows in ", file)
  field <- function(selector) html_text2(html_element(rows, selector))

  tibble(
    team = field(".name"), year = field(".year"),
    wins = field(".wins"), losses = field(".losses"),
    win_pct = field(".pct"), goals_for = field(".gf"),
    goals_against = field(".ga"),
    page_number = page_number, source_url = url
  )
}

hockey_raw <- bind_rows(lapply(page_numbers, scrape_hockey_page))
write_csv(hockey_raw, "data/raw/hockey_raw.csv")

retrievals <- bind_rows(lapply(page_numbers, function(p) {
  read_csv(file.path("data/raw", sprintf("page_%02d.html.csv", p)),
           show_col_types = FALSE)
}))
write_csv(retrievals, "results/retrieval_log.csv")

numeric_columns <- c("year", "wins", "losses", "win_pct",
                     "goals_for", "goals_against")
parsed <- hockey_raw |>
  mutate(team = trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ", team)),
         across(all_of(numeric_columns),
                ~ parse_number(.x, na = c("", "NA"))))

missing_row <- !complete.cases(parsed[, c("team", numeric_columns)]) |
  parsed$team == ""
missing_count <- sum(missing_row)
hockey <- parsed[!missing_row, ]
if (nrow(hockey) == 0) stop("No complete records remain.")
# One observation should represent one team in one season.
if (anyDuplicated(hockey[c("team", "year")])) {
  stop("Duplicate team-season records: inspect the saved pages.")
}
if (any(hockey$win_pct < 0 | hockey$win_pct > 1) ||
    any(hockey$goals_for < 0 | hockey$goals_against < 0) ||
    any(hockey$wins < 0 | hockey$losses < 0)) {
  stop("Invalid values: inspect the source data.")
}

hockey <- hockey |>
  mutate(goal_diff = goals_for - goals_against)
write_csv(hockey, "data/clean/hockey.csv")

comparison <- tibble(
  measure = c("Goals scored", "Goal differential"),
  correlation = c(cor(hockey$goals_for, hockey$win_pct),
                  cor(hockey$goal_diff, hockey$win_pct))
)
write_csv(comparison, "results/correlations.csv")

sample_summary <- tibble(
  pages_requested = length(page_numbers),
  scraped_rows = nrow(hockey_raw), incomplete_rows_removed = missing_count,
  analyzed_rows = nrow(hockey), first_year = min(hockey$year),
  last_year = max(hockey$year)
)
write_csv(sample_summary, "results/sample_summary.csv")
write_csv(count(hockey, year, name = "team_seasons"),
          "results/observations_by_year.csv")
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "results/sessionInfo.txt")

r_goals <- comparison$correlation[1]
r_diff <- comparison$correlation[2]
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
stronger <- if (r_diff > r_goals) "goal differential" else "goals scored"

p1 <- ggplot(hockey, aes(goals_for, win_pct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")) +
  labs(title = "Goals scored and winning percentage",
       subtitle = "One point = one team-season; line = fitted linear relationship",
       x = "Total goals scored in the season", y = "Winning percentage",
       caption = "Source: Scrape This Site, hockey pages 1–24.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p2 <- ggplot(hockey, aes(goal_diff, win_pct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")) +
  labs(title = "Goal differential and winning percentage",
       subtitle = "One point = one team-season; line = fitted linear relationship",
       x = "Goals scored minus goals allowed", y = "Winning percentage",
       caption = "Source: Scrape This Site, hockey pages 1–24.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggsave("figures/goals_scored.png", p1, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 180)
ggsave("figures/goal_differential.png", p2, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 180)

# Illustrative pair: same year and identical goals scored; largest win-rate gap.
# Record the selection rule so the example is not mistaken for a random sample.
pairs <- inner_join(
  hockey |> select(team, year, goals_for, win_pct),
  hockey |> select(team, year, goals_for, win_pct),
  by = c("year", "goals_for"), suffix = c("_a", "_b"),
  relationship = "many-to-many"
) |>
  filter(team_a < team_b) |>
  mutate(gap = abs(win_pct_a - win_pct_b)) |>
  arrange(desc(gap), year, team_a, team_b)
if (!nrow(pairs)) stop("No same-year, equal-scoring pair found.")
chosen <- slice_head(pairs, n = 1)
example <- hockey |>
  filter(year == chosen$year,
         team %in% c(chosen$team_a, chosen$team_b)) |>
  arrange(desc(win_pct))
stopifnot(nrow(example) == 2)
write_csv(example, "results/equal_scoring_example.csv")
write_csv(chosen, "results/example_selection.csv")
better <- example[1, ]
worse <- example[2, ]
percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```


Two NHL teams scored **`r better$goals_for` goals each**, yet one won **`r better$wins` games** and the other only **`r worse$wins`**. In the records labeled `r better$year`, the `r better$team` and `r worse$team` looked identical on scoring totals. Their results were far apart.

The difference becomes easier to understand when goals allowed enter the picture. The `r better$team` conceded `r better$goals_against` goals; the `r worse$team` conceded `r worse$goals_against`. That comparison raises a practical question: when reviewing a team's season, how much do we miss by looking at offense alone?

I scraped `r nrow(hockey)` team-season records from [Scrape This Site's hockey pages](https://www.scrapethissite.com/pages/forms/). In this sample, goal differential—goals scored minus goals allowed—has a much stronger relationship with winning percentage than scoring alone.

## Identical scoring totals, different seasons

```{r}
#| echo: false
example |>
  transmute(Team = team, `Goals scored` = goals_for,
            `Goals allowed` = goals_against, Wins = wins,
            `Winning percentage` = percent(win_pct)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste("Source: Scrape This Site; year label", better$year))
```

Minnesota's goal differential was +`r better$goal_diff`; Washington's was `r worse$goal_diff`. The winning percentages were `r percent(better$win_pct)` and `r percent(worse$win_pct)`, respectively. A ranking based only on goals scored would treat them as equals, missing a substantial difference in their records.

I selected the same-year, equal-scoring pair with the largest winning-percentage gap in the sample. It is a deliberately clear illustration, not a typical pair or proof that goals allowed caused the entire difference. The broader comparison below uses all the records.

## Scoring matters, but leaves plenty unexplained

```{r}
#| label: fig-goals
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The same season's total goals scored and reported winning percentage."
p1
```

Goals scored and winning percentage have a correlation of **`r fmt(r_goals)`**. The upward pattern makes sense, but the spread matters too: similar scoring totals occur alongside quite different winning percentages. For a quick review, I would treat goals scored as one piece of information rather than a complete assessment of performance.

Correlation ranges from −1 to 1. A value closer to 1 indicates a stronger positive linear relationship—not the percentage of wins explained or evidence of causation.

## Adding goals allowed brings the pattern into focus

```{r}
#| label: fig-differential
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Goal differential includes both scoring and goals allowed."
p2
```

For goal differential, the correlation rises to **`r fmt(r_diff)`**. Teams that outscored their opponents more heavily generally won a larger share of games in this sample.

This is not a surprising new law of hockey: scoring and conceding are directly connected to game outcomes. The useful finding is how much tighter the relationship becomes when both sides enter the comparison. It supports using goal differential as a first summary of a completed season, then checking offense and goals allowed separately.

## What I would do with this comparison

For a fan or analyst preparing a season review, I would use a two-step checklist: first compare teams' goal differentials within the same season; then inspect goals scored and allowed separately to explain the ranking. The opening table shows what an offense-only comparison misses, the first scatterplot shows that problem across the sample, and the second shows how adding goals allowed tightens the relationship. The recommendation concerns describing completed seasons, not choosing next year's players.

I would not use these correlations alone to predict next season or recommend a roster change. All measures describe the same completed seasons. The data pool different schedules and scoring environments, and total goals are not per-game rates. The teaching-site records have not been independently verified against official NHL statistics.

The takeaway is straightforward: **before calling a team strong because it scores a lot, check what it gives up.** That is a more useful way to read these results than treating the larger correlation as a forecasting model.

## Data, methods and reproducibility

I used `rvest` to collect the first 24 pages of a public scraping practice site. This is a subset, not a claim to cover every available record. New requests are spaced one second apart; saved HTML pages are reused on later renders. No login, CAPTCHA or paywall is bypassed.

After numeric conversion and removal of `r missing_count` incomplete rows, the sample contains `r nrow(hockey)` team-seasons with year labels `r min(hockey$year)`–`r max(hockey$year)`. I check duplicate team-year records and value ranges, retain the site's reported winning percentage, and calculate Pearson correlations. Retrieval dates and source URLs are saved with the data.

To reproduce this post, start with the [Post 2 README](https://github.com/ruibao1129/6400-rb/blob/main/blog/posts/post2/README.md), then open [index.qmd, the complete R analysis](https://github.com/ruibao1129/6400-rb/blob/main/blog/posts/post2/index.qmd). Source snapshots and raw data are in `data/raw`, cleaned data in `data/clean`, charts in `figures`, and correlations and the example-selection results in `results`. The `docs/` copy is generated website output, not the analysis entry point.
